opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I spent a lot of years before this working on robotics, and the thing that always struck me was that the hardest part was never really the motors or the mechanics. It was everything around common sense. Classical robotics is incredibly good at narrow, well-specified tasks: pick this exact part off a conveyor belt, put it in this exact spot. But the moment you step into the messy real world, you run into this long tail of situations that nobody programmed for. A box is upside down, someone left a cup in the way, the instructions are ambiguous. Historically, every one of those edge cases was another engineer writing another special-case rule, and that just doesn't scale.

What general-purpose language models give you is a kind of world knowledge and reasoning layer you didn't have to build yourself. They already know that cups hold liquid and you shouldn't tip them over, that "clean up the table" probably means dishes go to the sink and trash goes in the bin. That high-level task understanding and planning used to be the hard part, and suddenly it comes almost for free from training on all of human text.

The other big piece is the interface. You can just tell the robot what you want in plain language, and it can tell you what it's doing, or ask you a question when it's confused. That makes robots usable by normal people, not only robotics PhDs.

To be clear, it doesn't solve everything. Low-level control, dexterity, and getting reliable data from the physical world are still really hard, and that's where a lot of the remaining work is. But I think of it as the brain finally catching up. For decades, robotics was bottlenecked on intelligence and generalization, and now we have a general-purpose reasoning engine we can plug in. That changes the problem from "how do we hand-code every behavior" to "how do we connect this very capable model to the body," which is a much more tractable problem.

r001.rationale: The response says that coding special cases for the long tail does not scale, but does not compare the effort of fully specifying a task with performing it manually.

r002.rationale: It explains that models bring common-sense knowledge and high-level task understanding, reducing the need to hand-code every behavior or edge case.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I came to this from the robotics side first. Before Anthropic I co-founded Cobalt Robotics, where we built security robots that patrolled office buildings, and the thing that was always painful about robotics wasn't the hardware. Hardware is hard, but it's a known kind of hard. The real problem was that every robot was essentially a giant pile of brittle special cases. You'd write a behavior for "go check this door," and then a janitor leaves a mop bucket in the hallway and the whole thing falls apart, because the robot has no notion of what a mop bucket is or why it might be there or that it's totally fine to go around it.

What you actually want is common sense. You want the robot to understand the world the way a person understands it, so that when something novel happens, it can reason about it instead of hitting an exception handler. And for a long time that just wasn't available. You could train a model on your specific task, in your specific environment, and the moment anything shifted you were back to collecting data.

Language models change that because they're basically a compressed version of how humans talk about the world, and how humans talk about the world encodes an enormous amount of practical knowledge. If you ask a model "I'm a robot in a kitchen and I need to put the groceries away, where does the milk go," it knows the answer. Nobody labeled a robotics dataset for that. It just comes along for free from reading everything people have written. So the high-level planning and reasoning layer, which used to be this bespoke thing you'd rebuild for every deployment, suddenly becomes something you can get out of the box.

The other piece is that language is a really natural interface for the humans who have to work with these systems. A big part of why robots don't get deployed isn't capability, it's that a facilities manager can't tell the robot what to do without an engineer in the loop. If you can just say "skip the third floor tonight, they're doing construction," and it understands, that's a huge operational unlock.

Now, I want to be careful, because I don't think LLMs solve the low-level control problem. Getting a hand to grasp a wine glass without breaking it is still a perception and control problem, and language models are not going to do that for you directly. But they're great at being the thing that decides what to do and why, and at recovering gracefully when the plan goes wrong. Historically that layer was the one that broke most often and was hardest to make general. So I see it less as "language models will drive robots" and more as the missing brain-stem-to-cortex connection that lets all the other pieces finally be reused across tasks instead of rebuilt every time.

r001.rationale: The response describes brittle special cases and needing an engineer to direct robots, but does not say that fully specifying a task takes more effort than doing it manually.

r002.rationale: It says language models bring common sense and practical knowledge that lets robots reason about novel situations, reducing reliance on bespoke behaviors and programming for each deployment.

astra-6.text:
The big unlock is that you don’t have to learn everything from robot data anymore. Historically, if you wanted a robot to do a task, you’d build a fairly specialized system and collect data for that task. And then if you changed the task or the environment, a lot of that work didn’t transfer.

A general-purpose language model brings a lot of knowledge about the world with it. If you say, “Clean up the table,” it has some understanding of what that means: dishes probably go in the sink, trash goes in the bin, and you shouldn’t throw away someone’s laptop. You haven’t had to teach each of those concepts through robot demonstrations.

That doesn’t automatically solve the physical part. Grasping a slippery plate or figuring out whether something is about to fall still requires perception and control. But you can connect those capabilities to a system that understands the goal and can break it down into steps. That’s a really different starting point from programming every behavior by hand.

r001.rationale: The response describes task-specific system building and data collection as obstacles, but does not say that fully specifying a task takes more effort than doing it manually.

r002.rationale: It says a general-purpose language model brings world knowledge, giving examples such as where dishes and trash go, so those concepts need not be taught through robot demonstrations.

sol-6.1.text:
The big unlock is that you don’t have to train a separate model for every task. Traditionally, you’d build a robot to do one very specific thing, and getting it to do something slightly different could mean collecting a new dataset and doing a lot of engineering.

With a general-purpose language model, you start with something that already has a lot of knowledge about the world. You can say, “Clean up the table,” and it can break that down into steps, interpret what it sees, and decide which tools or robot actions to use. If something unexpected happens, it can reason about what to try next.

That doesn’t solve the physical control problem—you still need reliable perception and manipulation—but it gives you a much more general layer for connecting human intent to those capabilities. That’s what makes the possibility of a robot doing lots of different useful things feel much closer.

r001.rationale: It describes the data collection and engineering needed to adapt a robot to a different task, but does not say that fully specifying the task can take more effort than doing it manually.

r002.rationale: It says a general-purpose model brings knowledge about the world and can turn a broad instruction into steps and actions, conveying that less task detail needs to be explicitly programmed.
